entry.title: CDS joins you don't read: does HANA really skip them? (measured)
entry.content:
In my last post I checked if a WHERE on top of a CDS table function really reaches the table. This one goes the other way. Your view has three joins, and the consumer reads only one or two fields. Does HANA still execute all the joins?

Most of us answer this from memory: "HANA prunes unused joins", or "only with associations", or "only if you declare the cardinality". I wanted to see the plans, so I built a small lab on two releases.

The question

A view joins MARA with MAKT (texts) and T134 (material types). A report selects only the material number. Which joins does HANA really execute? And what happens to the result when the cardinality you declared is not true?

The setup

  • Systems: S/4HANA 2023 (SAP_BASIS 758, HANA 2.00.073) and S/4HANA 2020 (SAP_BASIS 755, HANA 2.00.052), both lab systems.
  • Data: the standard tables with the demo data that was already there. 2023: 1,199 materials and 2,051 material texts in 3 languages. 2020: 2,566 materials and 19,885 material texts in many languages.
  • Eight CDS view entities on MARA, changing only how the join is written:
  • ZJP_OUTER: LEFT OUTER JOIN to MAKT (language 'E' in the ON condition) and to T134, no cardinality.
  • ZJP_TOONE: the same with LEFT OUTER TO ONE JOIN.
  • ZJP_ASSOC: the same with association [0..1] and a path in the field list.
  • ZJP_INNER: INNER JOIN to T134.
  • ZJP_VIEW_OUTER: LEFT OUTER JOIN to a view entity on T134 instead of the table (VDM style), no cardinality.
  • ZJP_VIEW_TOONE: the same with LEFT OUTER TO ONE JOIN.
  • ZJP_TEXT: LEFT OUTER JOIN to MAKT without the language, no cardinality. One row per material and language, and the view says so.
  • ZJP_TEXT_ONE: association [0..1] to MAKT without the language. This cardinality is a lie: a material has one text per language.
  • Three consumer statements per view, in ABAP SQL: only Material, Material plus one joined field, and COUNT(*).
  • Method: rows counted in ABAP. For the plans I looked up the statement that ABAP SQL really sent in the HANA SQL plan cache and ran EXPLAIN PLAN FOR SQL PLAN CACHE ENTRY via ADBC. So each plan belongs to the real ABAP statement, not to a native SQL I typed by hand.

The results

Both releases gave the same plans. Rows are shown as 2023 / 2020.

ViewOnly MaterialMaterial + joined fieldCOUNT(*)Tables in the plan, only Material
ZJP_OUTER, no cardinality1,199 / 2,5661,199 / 2,5661,199 / 2,566MARA
ZJP_TOONE, to one1,199 / 2,5661,199 / 2,5661,199 / 2,566MARA
ZJP_ASSOC, [0..1]1,199 / 2,5661,199 / 2,5661,199 / 2,566MARA
ZJP_VIEW_OUTER, join to a view1,199 / 2,5661,199 / 2,5661,199 / 2,566MARA
ZJP_VIEW_TOONE1,199 / 2,5661,199 / 2,5661,199 / 2,566MARA
ZJP_INNER1,199 / 2,5661,199 / 2,5661,199 / 2,566MARA, T134
ZJP_TEXT, no language, no cardinality2,051 / 19,8852,051 / 19,8852,051 / 19,885MARA, MAKT
ZJP_TEXT_ONE, no language, [0..1]1,199 / 2,5662,051 / 19,8851,199 / 2,566MARA

The COUNT(*) plans follow the same pattern: MARA alone, except ZJP_INNER and ZJP_TEXT. With Material plus the text, ZJP_OUTER joins MAKT and still leaves T134 out.

Look at the last line. Same view, same WHERE (none), and the number of rows depends on the fields the consumer selects.

What the plans show

Simplified excerpts from the 2023 system. The 2020 system shows COLUMN SEARCH on MARA instead of TABLE SCAN, with the same tables.

ZJP_OUTER, only Material. Both joins are gone:

SELECT /* FDA READ */ "MATERIAL" FROM "ZJP_OUTER" WHERE "MANDT" = ?

PROJECT
  TABLE SCAN MARA

ZJP_OUTER, Material and text. MAKT comes back, T134 stays out:

COLUMN SEARCH
  JOIN
    COLUMN TABLE MARA
    COLUMN TABLE MAKT

ZJP_INNER, only Material. The join stays, because an inner join can remove rows:

COLUMN SEARCH
  JOIN
    COLUMN TABLE MARA
    COLUMN TABLE T134

ZJP_TEXT_ONE: with only Material, HANA reads MARA alone and returns 2,566 rows on 2020. Add the text and the join comes back with 19,885 rows, about 7.7 times more.

Where the cardinality goes

The SQL that activation generates for each view (ADT shows it) was the same on both releases:

  • LEFT OUTER JOIN without cardinality stays LEFT OUTER JOIN.
  • LEFT OUTER TO ONE JOIN and association [0..1] both become LEFT OUTER MANY TO ONE JOIN.
  • ZJP_TEXT_ONE also becomes LEFT OUTER MANY TO ONE JOIN, with only MANDT and MATNR in the ON condition. HANA has no way to know that this is false, so it trusts it.

Does anyone warn you?

  • 2023, association [0..1] without the language: activation passes with warning DD_CDS_ANALYSIS 302, "Cardinality 1 of Association _TEXT does not match to the ON-condition".
  • 2023, the same mistake written as LEFT OUTER TO ONE JOIN: no cardinality warning in the syntax check.
  • 2020: no warning for either version. The message text exists in the 2020 system, but the check did not fire for this view.

So the only warning I got was on the newer release, only for the association, and it is a warning: the view activates and runs.

Takeaways

  • HANA drops a LEFT OUTER JOIN you don't read when it can prove the join returns at most one row. Here it got that proof in two ways: the ON condition covered the whole primary key of the joined table (ZJP_OUTER needed no cardinality at all), or I declared it (TO ONE or [0..1]). A simple view entity in between did not stop it. My reading is that HANA used the primary keys of MAKT and T134; I did not test a join that is unique in the data but not by key.
  • An INNER JOIN is never dropped, even when you read nothing from it, because it can remove rows. If the lookup is optional, LEFT OUTER is not only the right semantics, it also lets HANA skip it.
  • When HANA cannot prove "to one" (ZJP_TEXT), it keeps the join. That is the safe default.
  • When you declare "to one" and it is not true, HANA believes you. The row count then depends on which fields the consumer selects: a list with the text shows 19,885 lines, the COUNT(*) on the same view says 2,566. For text associations, put the language in the ON condition (usually $session.system_language).

About time: with these small tables, the difference between a dropped and a kept join was below 1 ms per query and inside the noise of 10 runs, so I am not using time as the argument here. The gain grows with the size of the dropped tables, which I did not measure. The lie was visible in time on 2020: 3.7 ms for the 2,566 rows against 66.7 ms for the 19,885 rows (average of 10 runs with GET RUN TIME, including the transfer to ABAP).

The code

Views, with the annotations removed:

define view entity ZJP_OUTER
  as select from mara
    left outer join makt on  makt.matnr = mara.matnr
                         and makt.spras = 'E'
    left outer join t134 on t134.mtart = mara.mtart
{
  key mara.matnr as Material,
      mara.mtart as MaterialType,
      makt.maktx as MaterialText,
      t134.mtref as ReferenceType
}

// ZJP_TOONE: the same, with "left outer to one join" in both joins.

define view entity ZJP_ASSOC
  as select from mara
  association [0..1] to makt as _Text on  _Text.matnr = $projection.Material
                                      and _Text.spras = 'E'
  association [0..1] to t134 as _Type on _Type.mtart = $projection.MaterialType
{
  key mara.matnr  as Material,
      mara.mtart  as MaterialType,
      _Text.maktx as MaterialText,
      _Type.mtref as ReferenceType
}

define view entity ZJP_INNER
  as select from mara
    inner join t134 on t134.mtart = mara.mtart
{
  key mara.matnr as Material,
      mara.mtart as MaterialType,
      t134.mtref as ReferenceType
}

define view entity ZJP_TYPE
  as select from t134
{
  key mtart as MaterialType,
      mtref as ReferenceType
}

define view entity ZJP_VIEW_OUTER
  as select from mara
    left outer join ZJP_TYPE as Typ on Typ.MaterialType = mara.mtart
{
  key mara.matnr        as Material,
      mara.mtart        as MaterialType,
      Typ.ReferenceType as ReferenceType
}

// ZJP_VIEW_TOONE: the same, with "left outer to one join".

define view entity ZJP_TEXT
  as select from mara
    left outer join makt on makt.matnr = mara.matnr
{
  key mara.matnr as Material,
  key makt.spras as Language,
      mara.mtart as MaterialType,
      makt.maktx as MaterialText
}

define view entity ZJP_TEXT_ONE        // the lie: no language in the ON condition
  as select from mara
  association [0..1] to makt as _Text on _Text.matnr = $projection.Material
{
  key mara.matnr  as Material,
      mara.mtart  as MaterialType,
      _Text.maktx as MaterialText
}

How I read the plan of the real ABAP statement:

SELECT material FROM zjp_outer INTO TABLE @DATA(lt_rows).   " the consumer

" ADBC: find the statement in the plan cache and explain the cached plan
DATA(lo_st) = cl_sql_connection=>get_connection( )->create_statement( ).
" SELECT PLAN_ID FROM M_SQL_PLAN_CACHE
"  WHERE STATEMENT_STRING LIKE '%"ZJP_OUTER"%'
lo_st->execute_update( |EXPLAIN PLAN SET STATEMENT_NAME = 'JP1'| &&
                       | FOR SQL PLAN CACHE ENTRY { lv_plan_id }| ).
" SELECT OPERATOR_NAME, TABLE_NAME FROM EXPLAIN_PLAN_TABLE
"  WHERE STATEMENT_NAME = 'JP1'

Caveats

  • Two releases, lab systems, small demo data, one client each. I could not reach a 2025 system (SAP_BASIS 816) for this round.
  • Simple joins only. The view on the right side was a plain projection. VDM views with unions, aggregations or their own joins on the right side were not tested.
  • The LEFT OUTER TO ONE JOIN version of the lie was only syntax checked, not activated and run. That syntax generates the same MANY TO ONE join (see ZJP_TOONE), so I expect the same behavior, but I did not measure it.
  • Plans come from EXPLAIN PLAN (the optimizer). I did not use PlanViz.
  • HANA Cloud and the BTP ABAP Environment were not tested.

Your turn

Have you seen a "to one" join that HANA did not drop? Or a KPI that did not match the list behind it because of a cardinality? I would like to compare notes, especially on 2025 and on HANA Cloud.

entry.title: SAP HANA Data Provisioning Agent 2.8.1.2 on SLES 15.6 Installation and Connection to SAP HANA Cloud
entry.content:
The SAP HANA Data Provisioning Agent (DP Agent) is the on-premise component of SAP HANA smart data integration (SDI). It lets SAP HANA Cloud reach data sources inside your own network, for example to create virtual tables.

In this guide I install the DP Agent on SLES 15 SP6 and connect its configuration tool to an SAP HANA Cloud database. Registering the agent is not covered, for the reason explained at the end.

Lab environment

  • SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 15 SP6 (VM)
  • SAP HANA Data Provisioning Agent 2.8.1.2, Linux x86_64
  • SAP HANA Cloud free tier instance in an SAP BTP trial account

Step 1 – Create the SAP HANA Cloud instance

In the SAP BTP cockpit, open Service Marketplace, search for hana and choose SAP HANA Cloud .

 

Create an instance with the plan hana-free, runtime Cloud Foundry and a name of your choice.

In the Parameters step I set memory, systempassword and edition. The system password is the one used for DBADMIN later.

 

In my lab the name is hdb. Wait until the instance status is Usable.

 

 

Step 2 – Subscribe to SAP HANA Cloud tools

SAP HANA Cloud Central needs its own subscription. Without it you see No subscription.

 

Subscribe to SAP HANA Cloud with the plan tools, then choose Go to Application.

 

Step 3 – Assign the role collections

Without the SAP HANA Cloud role collections, SAP HANA Cloud Central answers Not authorized.

 

.In the cockpit open Security, Users, select your user and choose Assign Role Collection .

 

Sign out and sign in again afterwards.

Step 4 – Register the instance and prepare access

The instance now appears in SAP HANA Cloud Central as Running, Free tier.

 

Register it with the DBADMIN user.

Copy the SQL endpoint of the instance (Actions, Copy SQL Endpoint). You need it in Step 7.

 

Under Manage Configuration, Connections, choose Allow all IP addresses for the lab.

 

For anything beyond a lab, allow only your trusted IP range.

Under User Management, create a database user for the agent messaging. In my lab it is DPA_MSG_USER .

 

I did not grant it any additional privileges.

Step 5 – Download the DP Agent

Download the SDI Data Provisioning Agent for Linux x86_64 from the SAP Development Tools page, Cloud Integration tab.

 

Step 6 – Install the DP Agent on SLES

Unzip the installer and create a dedicated OS user and group:

 
bash
zypper install -y unzip
unzip installer.DPAgent-2.8.1.2-final-1-linuxx86_64.zip
groupadd -f dpagent
useradd -g dpagent -m -s /bin/bash dpagent
passwd dpagent

Create the target directory. Move the installer out of /root, because the dpagent user cannot read it there, and hand over the ownership:

 
bash
mkdir -p /usr/sap/dataprovagent
chown -R dpagent:dpagent /usr/sap/dataprovagent
mv /root/sapmedia/HANA_DP_AGENT_20_LIN_X86_64 /tmp/
chown -R dpagent:dpagent /tmp/HANA_DP_AGENT_20_LIN_X86_64
chmod -R 755 /tmp/HANA_DP_AGENT_20_LIN_X86_64

Switch to the agent user and start the installer:

 
bash
su - dpagent
cd /tmp/HANA_DP_AGENT_20_LIN_X86_64
./hdbinst

I accepted the defaults: installation path /usr/sap/dataprovagent, listener port 5050, administration port 5051 and the bundled JRE. The installer ends with Installation done.

 

The installer notes that the default settings use an insecure channel to the HANA server and that SSL must be configured afterwards. I kept the defaults for this lab.

Step 7 – Connect the configuration tool to SAP HANA Cloud

Start the configuration tool as the dpagent user:

 
bash
cd /usr/sap/dataprovagent/bin
./agentcli.sh --configAgent

Check that the agent runs with option 1, Agent Status, or start it with option 2, Start or Stop Agent. Then choose option 7, Connect the Configuration Tool to SAP HANA, and option 1, Connect to SAP HANA Cloud via JDBC .

 

Enter:

Prompt Value
Use encrypted JDBC connectiontrue
Host nameyour SQL endpoint, without the port
Port443
Use X509 client certificate (admin user)false
Agent admin HANA userDBADMIN
Use X509 client certificate (messaging user)false
HANA user for agent messagingDPA_MSG_USER
Use proxy serverfalse
Create a new SAP HANA userfalse, the user already exists

The tool answers Agent configuration tool is connected to SAP HANA server via JDBC.

Where this stops

Registering the agent option failed in my lab with:

 
text
SAP DBTech JDBC: [403]: internal error: Cannot connect to agent: dpagent_scc at <agent host>:5050
Context: Cannot connect to hdbdpserver

SAP KBA 3751584 describes this symptom and points to the dpserver service of the database not running. In SAP HANA Cloud Central, the Data Provisioning Server option under Advanced Settings is unchecked on my free tier instance, and I could not select it. SAP HANA Cloud Central also states that not all advanced options are available for free tier instances. I have not confirmed that the free tier is the cause, so I am not drawing that conclusion here.

I will continue with the registration and the adapters in a later post. If you have enabled the Data Provisioning Server on a free tier instance, I would be glad to hear how in the comments.

Conclusion

In this guide I prepared an SAP HANA Cloud free tier instance, installed the SAP HANA Data Provisioning Agent 2.8.1.2 on SLES 15 SP6, and connected the agent configuration tool to the database via JDBC.

A few points are worth remembering if you try the same:

  • SAP HANA Cloud Central needs its own tools subscription and the SAP HANA Cloud role collections. Missing either one shows up as No subscription or Not authorized.
  • Run the installer as a dedicated dpagent user, and keep the installer files somewhere that user can read.
  • When you copy commands from a terminal, leave the prompt out. A pasted > can overwrite a script.
  • The configuration tool connecting successfully does not mean the agent can be registered. Registration also needs the Data Provisioning Server of the database, and on my free tier instance I could not enable it.

entry.title: A Battery Recall, a Graph, and an AI Agent
entry.content:
This is a personal portfolio project exploring graph capabilities of the SAP HANA database. It tries to answer two questions: can a graph find everyone affected by a motorcycle battery recall, and can an AI Agent make a sensible remedy plan when replacement battery packs are scarce.

 

I asked Claude Code (Opus 5.5) what would be a good showcase for a graph. He suggested we do a spike first: a quick, throwaway experiment to see whether an idea holds water before anyone builds anything.

 

Spike one: The where-used index

The first candidate was ABAP's own where-used index. Table WBCROSSGT has 9.7 million rows on my A4H, and as a graph of who uses which type it came to 205,145 vertices and 1,017,224 edges. Unknown depth, cycles, the lot. Surely a job for a graph?

Turns out, not really. A plain ABAP loop of about 25 lines (level by level, SELECT ... FOR ALL ENTRIES, a hashed table of what it had already seen) found exactly the same objects in all four test cases, within about 2 seconds and with no setup. Warm, the graph was 3 to 8 times faster, but building it cold took 7 to 14 seconds. And the one job that should have been its home turf, finding cycles, gave no answer after 9 minutes, so we aborted it.

So much for that.

 

Spike two: The real-life project

Then I remembered a project I once did.

  • A manufacturing component is found to be defective.
  • Find all production orders where it was used,
  • then find the subsequent production orders where the material produced in the previous one was used as a component (several levels deep),
  • then find the sales orders where it was sold,
  • then find out whether it was shipped to a customer or is still at a storage location.

The objective: notify the customer and send them a replacement, or take the product out of the storage location and scrap it.

Would that have been a good case for a graph? We had no data to try it on. So we invented some, and gave it a home in my Supply Chain Rescue demo app, which already has a fictional maker of electric motorcycles. Electric motorcycles have batteries. Batteries have cell lots. You can see where this is going.

A second spike on that idea went better, so we built the real thing: Recall Rescue.

 

The battery genealogy

Claude generated 12 weeks of motorcycle production and sales, from week 28 of 2026, with a battery genealogy behind every one of them:

  • a cell lot from the supplier VoltCell goes into battery modules,
  • modules go into packs,
  • packs go into motorcycles, or wait at the service stock as spare packs,
  • motorcycles go to customers, or wait at a plant, a dealer or the service stock.

That alone would be a tree: every module sits in one pack and every pack in one motorcycle, so from any module there is exactly one way forward. What breaks the simple tree is reuse and remanufacturing:

  • On 1 September, 8 private motorcycles from week 29 got a new pack.
  • Their old packs were taken apart, and 2 modules each from 2 old packs made one remanufactured pack.

So now a module has two links:

  1. the old one to the pack it came from,
  2. the new one to the remanufactured pack.

On 21 September, 3 of the remanufactured packs went into motorcycles sold in weeks 31 to 35, under warranty. The old links stay in the database as history, marked inactive, and that will matter in a minute.

A perfect setup to declare one lot defective and try to trace it.

Side note: the EU thinks along the same lines. From 18 February 2027 every LMT and electric vehicle battery placed on the EU market, electric motorcycle batteries included, needs a battery passport, and a remanufactured battery gets "a new battery passport linked to the battery passport or passports of the original battery or batteries" (Article 77 of Regulation (EU) 2023/1542). Recall Rescue doesn't build passports, mind you, but the links behind them make a graph for the same reason the workshop does here.

 

All in all 27,814 items and 42,487 links in two Database Tables in A4H, generated from a fixed seed, so the world comes out the same every time.

 

Four lines of openCypher

If you haven't met openCypher yet: it's a query language for graphs, the open version of Cypher, which came from Neo4j. Where SQL makes you join tables, openCypher has you draw the pattern you're looking for, in ASCII art. (a) is a node, -[r]-> is a relationship pointing from one node to the next, and [*1..4] means 1 to 4 relationships, whatever lies in between (the part that takes a loop in ABAP).

  • MATCH draws the pattern,
  • WHERE filters it,
  • RETURN says what you want back.

HANA understands a subset of it and runs it against a graph workspace.

The question for a recall is: who has a battery with cells from this lot, right now? In openCypher it reads almost like the sentence (RETURN trimmed):

MATCH p = (l)-[*1..4]->(u), (u)-[h]->(t)
WHERE l.VERTEXID = 'LOT-VC-W29-03' AND (u.KIND = 'VIN' OR u.KIND = 'PACK') AND (t.KIND = 'CUST' OR t.KIND = 'SLOC')
  AND h.ACTIVE = 'X' AND ALL(e IN RELATIONSHIPS(p) WHERE e.ACTIVE = 'X')
RETURN u.VERTEXID AS UNIT, t.VERTEXID AS HOLDER

Start at the lot, follow 1 to 4 links to a motorcycle or a pack, then one more link to whoever holds it - a customer or a storage location. Current links only.

That last condition is important. For the lot LOT-VC-W29-03 the trace finds 27 units with their holders. Let it follow the history too, and it finds 35: Eight customers would get a recall notice for a battery that isn't in their motorcycle any more.

This is what the trace has to walk through: the whole family tree of LOT-VC-W29-03, straight from the vertex and edge tables, history and all. The red dashed links are the 8 packs the workshop took out, and the grey motorcycles are the 8 customers who would get a notice for nothing:

And this is what the four lines of openCypher make of it, as the app draws their answer: 27 units with their holders, 4 of them through the remanufactured packs, and not one of the 8 grey motorcycles:

How do I know the graph isn't just confidently wrong? Claude also wrote an oracle: a plain JavaScript walk over the same items and links, level by level, with no graph anywhere. For all 8 standard lots of week 29 the two agree exactly, unit by unit and holder by holder.

And speed? Doesn't matter at this size. In the spike the ABAP loop took 77 ms and the graph 67 ms. Now a warm trace answers in about 400 to 800 ms, through OData and all. Here is a screenshot from Postman:

 

The catch

There is one, and it's big if you live in ABAP Cloud.

  • The trace runs on A4H's own HANA, over a graph workspace that an AMDP method defines on two CDS view entities.
  • But openCypher won't go through an AMDP. ABAP's check rejects the SQL that HANA expands the query into: "The ABAP database schema ... cannot be specified explicitly". Uwe Fetzer ( @UweFetzer_se38 ) reported exactly this back in 2019, in his SAP Community question Opencypher in AMDP, and SAP called it a bug. I hit the same error on my release 816 system.
  • What does work is native SQL through ADBC (cl_sql_statement): SELECT ... FROM OPENCYPHER_TABLE( GRAPH WORKSPACE ... QUERY '...' ). ADBC is not released for ABAP Cloud, so this is classic ABAP only.
  • No query parameters either. The lot goes into the query text, so it's checked against a strict pattern first, and nothing but a lot number of the form LOT-VC-W29-03 gets through.
  • HANA 2.00.087 speaks a subset of openCypher: no named variable-length edge like [e*1..4], and one hop per pattern element. Hence the comma in the MATCH above.

The trace is a RAP custom entity, so to everyone else it's just another OData entity set.

 

Inside ZCL_RR_TRACE

The whole graph part lives in one class, ZCL_RR_TRACE. The graph itself is ten lines of it, an AMDP method that says which CDS view entity holds the vertices and which the edges:

METHOD graph BY DATABASE GRAPH WORKSPACE FOR HDB
  LANGUAGE SQL
  USING zi_rr_graphedge zi_rr_graphvertex.
  edge table zi_rr_graphedge
    source column sourceid
    target column targetid
    key    column edgeid
  vertex table zi_rr_graphvertex
    key    column vertexid
ENDMETHOD.

ZI_RR_GraphVertex reads the items, ZI_RR_GraphEdge the links. No copy of the data, no extra tables. Apart from that, the class does three jobs:

  1. It wakes the graph up. HANA creates an AMDP graph workspace only the first time an AMDP uses it, and our query comes in through ADBC. So before every query a tiny GraphScript procedure (HANA's own graph language) counts the vertices. The count goes nowhere - it's the wake-up call.
  2. It asks the question. Method UNITS checks the lot against the pattern, writes the four lines of openCypher into a string, wraps them in SELECT ... FROM OPENCYPHER_TABLE( GRAPH WORKSPACE "ZCL_RR_TRACE=>GRAPH" QUERY '...' ) and runs that through cl_sql_statement. The graph answers with units and holders only. Plain ABAP SQL then adds the model, the pack type, the delivery date, the current pack and the modules for the route text.
  3. It serves OData. The class implements IF_RAP_QUERY_PROVIDER, which makes it the query behind the custom entity ZI_RR_Trace. It takes exactly two filters, LotId eq and WithHistory eq, refuses any sorting, and does the paging itself.

 

The rest of the plumbing

Around the trace:

  • a RAP business object for the recall, in A4H: declare a lot defective, own the affected units (so two recalls never fight over one motorcycle), apply a remedy plan all or nothing,
  • in CAP, the plan and its rules: spare packs are scarce, so customers come first, and no motorcycle in stock gets a pack while a customer waits for one,
  • a Recall Agent who proposes a plan, explains it, and waits for an approver before anything reaches A4H,
  • a Recall section in the app, with the trace drawn as a graph and a button that opens the existing battery shortage scenario. One defect, two directions: back to who is affected, forward to what the shortage stops.

This is the trace of LOT-VC-W29-03 in the app, with the fleet customer CUS-FLEET-2 clicked: its routes light up in blue and everything else fades. 3 motorcycles, one of them through the remanufactured pack PCK-R0002, whose line stays orange. The modules are tucked into the lines from the lot to the packs:

In the first end-to-end run, the Recall Agent (Claude Sonnet 5) got LOT-VC-W29-03: 23 customer motorcycles, 3 in stock, 1 spare pack, 4 routes through remanufactured packs, and 16 free spare packs to go round. About 50 seconds later he was waiting for approval, with a plan:

  • 16 customers get a replacement pack now,
  • 7 get a notice and wait,
  • the 3 motorcycles in stock are blocked,
  • the affected spare pack is scrapped,
  • 10 packs need new supply from VoltCell, which in the Supply Chain Rescue world is blocked.

He also explained why one of the 6 fleet motorcycles, delivered two weeks after the other 5, doesn't jump the queue: "bumping it ahead of earlier-committed customers isn't justified by any stated operational need".

On the trace, a plan shows in colour: green gets a new pack now, purple waits for new supply, with the delivery date that decides who comes first. This is the bottom of the motorcycles column for that plan, the same as the rule plan. VIN-CARGO-31034, delivered on 6 August, waits in purple, while the other fleet motorcycles from 23 July get their packs:

Did the Agent do anything the rule plan didn't? Not this time: 0 units differ. After Approve, the plan was applied in A4H in 5.5 seconds.

Then Claude ran it again for the screenshots: same lot, same world, same Model. And this time that fleet motorcycle did jump the queue:

 

2 units differ from the rule plan: the fleet motorcycle VIN-CARGO-31034 got PCK-003635, the pack the rule plan gives to VIN-CITY-29118, and VIN-CITY-29118 waits instead. The Agent's reason: fleet vehicles "see higher daily mileage/usage and are safety-prioritized for scarce replacement packs ahead of equally-dated non-fleet customers".

Equally dated? VIN-CITY-29118 was delivered on 23 July, VIN-CARGO-31034 on 6 August. And Approve? Claude clicked it, taking the screenshots for me in the browser, without checking the dates either.

So which rule did the Agent break? None, strictly speaking. The delivery date is only the order the rule plan goes by. What the app enforces is that customers come before motorcycles in stock and that no spare pack sits idle while someone waits, and A4H checks the rest when the plan is applied. Fleet first is even allowed: the Agent's instructions say he may change which customers get the scarce packs, "for example fleet motorcycles in daily use first", as long as he explains every difference from the rule plan. He did explain it. The explanation was just wrong.

What could be changed after seeing this? For example: show the delivery dates of the units that differ on the card, have CAP check the dates the rationale claims, or leave the app as it is and make sure a person reads the units that differ.

 

So, was the graph useful?

Not because of speed. At this size it decides nothing, and a plain loop keeps up. On the query, the recall question is four lines of openCypher, and the difference between the right notices and 8 wrong ones on top is one condition in those four lines. The catch is the platform: classic ABAP only, through native SQL, until the AMDP bug is fixed.

And the Agent? He made a plan that passed every rule, in about 50 seconds, and in one of two runs explained it with dates that weren't true. The rules caught nothing because nothing was broken. The reason would still probably need a person who checks it against the data, thought.

 

P.S.: The setup was A4H, the 2025 Developer Trial (release 816 on HANA 2.00.087), in Docker on a VPS, reached through an SSH tunnel, and a Mac. Claude Code ran Opus 5.5 as the main Agent, with Haiku, Sonnet and Opus 5.5 sub-Agents, and talked to A4H through the vibing-steampunk MCP Server by Alice Vinogradova. Supply Chain Rescue runs CAP 10.1 on Node 24 and SAPUI5 1.136.8. The code: github.com/Kamilkov/supply-chain-rescue.

entry.title: Configuring SSL Encryption Between SAP ABAP Application Servers and SAP HANA
entry.content:
Introduction

This blog documents the steps required to configure SSL/TLS encryption between SAP ABAP application servers and an SAP HANA database, using a certificate signed by an external Certificate Authority (CA). This is a common requirement in enterprise migrations and security hardening projects where the default SAP-generated certificates are replaced with organisation-specific ones.

The configuration covered here implements TLS — the HANA database server authenticates itself to the ABAP application layer. sapcli.pse on each ABAP node serves as the trust store, allowing the ABAP kernel to verify HANA's certificate during the TLS handshake. This guide assumes you are working on a Linux-based SAP system with SAP CommonCryptoLib installed.

Prerequisites

  • Database certificate (.pfx format) signed by an external CA, plus the corresponding root certificate
  • Certificate password
  • Access to the HANA database server at OS level (sidadm or equivalent)
  • Access to all ABAP application server nodes at OS level
  • A valid HANA userstore key configured for hdbsql commands
  • Planned downtime or maintenance window — the ABAP application must be stopped during parts of this procedure
  • Existing SAPSSLS.pse backed up before making any changes

Overview

The procedure creates two sets of PSE (Personal Security Environment) files:

  1. SAPSSLS.pse on the HANA server — the HANA database server's SSL identity, built from the externally signed certificate. This is what HANA presents to the ABAP layer during the TLS handshake.

  2. sapcli.pse and sapsrv.pse on each ABAP application server — these are placed in the sec directory of each ABAP node. They act as the trust store on the ABAP side, containing the CA certificate chain that the ABAP kernel uses to verify HANA's certificate. The sslKeyStore reference in the profile parameter also points to sapcli.pse, but since sslclientpki is off on HANA, the client certificate is never requested.

Step 1 — Upload Certificates to the HANA Server

  1. Log on to the HANA database server at OS level as sidadm
  2. Upload the database certificate (db_cert.pfx), the root certificate (root.cer) (and any intermediate certificates) to the sec directory on the HANA server:
/usr/sap/<SID>/SYS/global/security/rsecssls/

Note: The exact sec directory path may vary. Confirm the location using the SECUDIR environment variable.

  1. Before making any changes, back up the existing SAPSSLS.pse:
cp SAPSSLS.pse SAPSSLS.pse.bak

Step 2 — Create SAPSSLS.pse on the HANA Server

Run the following command to create a new SAPSSLS.pse from the externally signed certificate. This becomes the HANA server's SSL identity:

sapgenpse import_p12 -r root.cer -p SAPSSLS.pse <db_cert.pfx>
  • Enter the certificate password when prompted
  • When asked for a PIN, you have the option to set one or leave it empty. From a security perspective, setting a PIN is recommended as it adds an additional layer of protection to the PSE file. If a PIN is set, ensure it is stored securely as it will be required for any future PSE operations

SAPSSLS.pse should now be created successfully.

Step 3 — Create the Client PSE Files for ABAP Application Servers

sapcli.pse and sapsrv.pse can be created directly from SAPSSLS.pse:

cp SAPSSLS.pse sapcli.pse
cp SAPSSLS.pse sapsrv.pse

Copy both files to the sec directory on every ABAP application server node (CS/CI and all additional application servers):

/usr/sap/<SID>/<instance_dir>/sec/

Step 4 — Disable sslclientpki on HANA

Important: Shut down the ABAP application layer before executing this step.

This parameter controls whether HANA enforces client PKI certificate authentication. Setting it to off enables one-way TLS (server authentication only), which is the configuration used here.

Run the following hdbsql command from the HANA server:

hdbsql -U <USERSTORE_KEY> "ALTER SYSTEM ALTER CONFIGURATION ('global.ini', 'SYSTEM') SET ('communication', 'sslclientpki') = 'off' WITH RECONFIGURE;"

The WITH RECONFIGURE clause applies the change immediately without requiring a HANA restart.

PRD Systems: This parameter must also be disabled on the secondary/DR HANA node. This can be done via SAP HANA Studio — apply the change on both the primary and DR secondary database nodes.

Step 5 — Configure the ABAP Default Profile

The dbs/hdb/connect_property parameter must be added to the ABAP default profile (DEFAULT.PFL) to instruct the ABAP kernel to use SSL when connecting to HANA. This parameter applies to all application server instances.

Add the following parameter (adapt values to your system):

dbs/hdb/connect_property = ENCRYPT=TRUE,sslCryptoProvider=commoncrypto,sslKeyStore=/usr/sap/<SID>/<instance_dir>/sec/sapcli.pse,sslTrustStore=/usr/sap/<SID>/<instance_dir>/sec/sapcli.pse,sslHostNameInCertificate=<hana_hostname>.<yourdomain.com>

Key values to adapt:

  • <SID> — your system ID
  • <instance_dir> — the instance directory of each application server (e.g. D00, D01)
  • <hana_hostname>.<yourdomain.com> — the fully qualified hostname as it appears in the HANA certificate's CN/SAN field

Note: The sslHostNameInCertificate value must match exactly what is embedded in the HANA server certificate, otherwise the SSL handshake will fail.

Step 6 — Restart the Application and Validate

Start the ABAP application layer. Once all instances are up, perform the following validation steps.

Validation 1 — Check encrypted connections via SQL

Log on to the system and navigate to transaction DB02 → SQL Editor. Run the following statement, replacing <SCHEMA> with the correct database schema name:

SELECT IS_ENCRYPTED, SSL_VERSION, CLIENT_HOST
FROM SYS.M_CONNECTIONS
WHERE USER_NAME = '<SCHEMA>'
AND IS_ENCRYPTED = 'TRUE';

All active connections for the schema should return TRUE in the IS_ENCRYPTED column. If any sessions return FALSE, review the profile parameter and PSE file placement.

Validation 2 — R3trans connectivity check

Run the following from the OS level on each application server to confirm no transport-layer issues:

R3trans -d

Review the trans.log output — a clean run with no errors confirms successful connectivity between the ABAP application layer and HANA over SSL.

Summary

At this point, SSL encryption between the SAP ABAP application servers and SAP HANA is active using an externally signed CA certificate. The HANA server authenticates to the application layer via SAPSSLS.pse, while each ABAP node uses sapcli.pse and sapsrv.pse as its trust store for verifying HANA's identity.
